summary: Describes extensions to LSP ping so it can verify connectivity and trace routes for MPLS Transport Profile LSPs and pseudowires on demand. It also clarifies how related operations messages should be handled. It updates RFC 4379.

plainLanguage.summary: A technician sometimes needs to check if a line works, right now. This extends the network version of a ping so it can test transport-style paths and show the route taken.

questions: how to trace route in mpls-tp
what is mpls-tp on-demand connectivity verification
how does route tracing work in mpls-tp
subtitle: How to extend LSP ping so operators can test and trace MPLS Transport Profile paths, even without IP addresses.

tldr.problem: LSP ping checks MPLS paths but relies on IP addressing, which MPLS Transport Profile (MPLS-TP) networks may not have or want to use.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC adds a Non IP address type, Source and Destination Identifier TLVs, new sub-TLVs for static LSPs and pseudowires, and a new Associated Channel Type so echo requests and replies can travel without IP or UDP headers.
tldr.outcome: Operators can run on-demand connectivity verification and route tracing on MPLS-TP LSPs and pseudowires with or without IP. The RFC updates RFC 4379.

today: RFC 6426 is a Proposed Standard, published November 2011. It updates RFC 4379 by adding a new address type and creating an IANA registry, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Introduction and Terms
sections.content:
LSP ping (RFC 4379) is an Operations, Administration, and Maintenance (OAM) tool for MPLS Label Switched Paths (LSPs). This RFC extends it so it can do on-demand monitoring of MPLS Transport Profile (MPLS-TP) LSPs and pseudowires, and it clarifies how the related OAM packets are processed.

It covers two functions required by RFC 5860 and specified in RFC 6371: on-demand connectivity verification (CV) and route tracing. The document calls the sender of a request the Requester and the node that answers the Responder. A Responder is not always at the egress of the LSP, because it may receive a request when the time-to-live (TTL) expires.
sections.plainLanguage: Someone sends a test message down a path, and whoever receives it sends an answer back. The sender is the Requester and the answerer is the Responder.

sections.title: Why IP Is Not Always Wanted
sections.content:
Ordinary LSP ping wraps each packet in an IP and UDP header with a destination address from the 127/8 range, then in the MPLS label stack. A Responder spots OAM packets by that 127/8 address and the UDP port number. This does not need IP forwarding, but it does need an IP host stack on each responding node.

In some MPLS-TP deployments IP addressing might not be available, or a non-IP encapsulation might be preferred. In that case on-demand CV and route tracing SHOULD run without IP addressing, using the Associated Channel (ACH). When IP addressing is used, as in non MPLS-TP LSPs, the procedures of RFC 4379 MUST be used.
sections.plainLanguage: Normally the test message has a street address on it. Some networks have no street addresses, so the message needs another way to find its way and be recognised.

sections.title: New Addresses, Identifiers and Sub-TLVs
sections.content:
The RFC defines a new Downstream Mapping address type, type 5 "Non IP" (12 octets). It can be used in any Downstream Mapping (DSMAP) or Downstream Detailed Mapping (DDMAP, RFC 6424) TLV. No address is carried, but the ingress and egress IF_Num values and multipath information are. A value of zero means no interface applies. Multipath Type SHOULD be zero, and the receiver MUST bypass interface verification and only do label control-plane and data-plane consistency checks. If both IF_Num fields are non-zero and either is wrong for the LSP or pseudowire, the Responder sends Return Code 5 (Downstream Mapping Mis-match).

Two new identifier TLVs, Source Identifier (type 13) and Destination Identifier (type 14), each have length 8 and carry a Global_ID and Node_ID of 4 octets each, as defined in RFC 6370. A packet MUST NOT include more than one of each. If it does, error 1 (Malformed echo request received) MUST be returned when the source can be identified unambiguously.

To name statically provisioned paths in the Target FEC Stack TLV, there are two new sub-TLVs: sub-type 22 for a Static LSP (length 24) and sub-type 23 for a Static Pseudowire (length 32). The Static LSP value holds source and destination Global ID and Node ID plus tunnel numbers and an LSP number. The Static Pseudowire value holds a 64-bit Service Identifier plus source and destination Global ID, Node ID and AC-ID. Global IDs MAY be zero, which means not applicable.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC adds new name tags: one says who sent the test, one says who it is for, and two describe the exact fixed path being tested. There is also a way to say no street address is used.

sections.title: On-Demand Connectivity Verification
sections.content:
A new Pseudowire Associated Channel Type, 0x0025, marks on-demand CV packets. ACH TLVs SHALL NOT be associated with it. To probe an intermediate point, the MPLS label TTL MUST be set so that it expires at the node to probe. At the Requester, a Generic Associated Channel Label (GAL) MUST be added before the MPLS LSP label. The GAL is not part of the label stack the Responder verifies, so no Nil FEC TLV is attached to it, and it MUST NOT appear in DSMAP or DDMAP TLVs.

There are three ways to send a request. With plain IP encapsulation, the reply MUST go on the reverse path of the LSP with IP and UDP headers. With IP encapsulation over ACH, the IP ACH type of RFC 4385 MUST be used and the reply SHOULD use ACH and be IP encapsulated. In the non-IP case the payload MUST directly follow the ACH header, the reply mode SHOULD be 4 (reply via application level control channel), and IP and UDP headers MUST NOT be attached. If a node cannot reply in the requested mode it MUST drop the request and send no response.

Point-to-multipoint LSPs follow RFC 6425 with IP, and the non-IP procedure can be applied when IP is not used.
sections.plainLanguage: You can send the test message three ways: with a full address, with an address inside a special lane, or with no address at all. The answer comes back along the same path in the other direction.

sections.title: Reverse-Path Verification and Route Tracing
sections.content:
A new Global flag, Validate Reverse Path (R), is defined in the LSP ping header. When set in an echo request, the Responder SHOULD attach a Reverse-path Target FEC Stack TLV (type 16) to the reply. The R flag MUST NOT be set in the echo response. For co-routed bidirectional LSPs the reverse stack is the same as the forward one; for associated bidirectional LSPs it MAY differ. On receiving the response, the Requester MUST validate the interface and label stack and, if the TLV is present, the FEC. On any failure it MUST drop the response and SHOULD log or report an error.

For route tracing the Requester includes a Downstream Mapping TLV, and MPLS TTL expiry directs packets to specific nodes along the path. Without IP, the address type can be set to Non IP. In the non-IP case responses are received on the LSP itself and identified by the on-demand CV channel type in the ACH header. If the Responder cannot identify the LSP for its reply, it MUST drop the request and send nothing.

Using ACH on-demand CV SHOULD NOT be done when the LSP has equal cost multipath (ECMP), because the extra ACH header can change the hashing for OAM packets and give an incorrect picture of the path data traffic takes.
sections.plainLanguage: A flag can ask the answerer to also describe the path back, so the sender can check both directions. To find the route, the sender sends tests that run out of time at each stop, so each stop answers in turn.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC introduces no new security considerations of its own; those in RFC 4379 apply. It notes, however, that on-demand CV for transport paths may well be used across MPLS administrative boundaries. In that case it is RECOMMENDED that on-demand OAM is configured so that Source Identifier TLVs are included in messages. That lets implementations filter OAM messages arriving from an unexpected or unknown source.
sections.plainLanguage: If test messages can come from other companies' networks, put a name tag on them so you can ignore strangers.

sections.title: IANA Assignments
sections.content:
IANA assigned TLV types 13 (Source ID) and 14 (Destination ID), Target FEC sub-types 22 (Static LSP) and 23 (Static Pseudowire), TLV type 16 (Reverse-path Target FEC Stack), and PW ACH type 0x0025 (On-Demand CV). Sub-types for the Target FEC Stack TLV and the Reverse-path Target FEC Stack TLV MUST be kept the same.

Because RFC 4379 defined Downstream Mapping address types without a registry, IANA also created a new Downstream Mapping Address Type registry, with allocation policy Standards Action. It starts with 1 IPv4 Numbered, 2 IPv4 Unnumbered, 3 IPv6 Numbered, 4 IPv6 Unnumbered and 5 Non IP.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC asked the official number-keeper to reserve some numbers for the new things, and to start a proper list of address kinds so numbers never clash.

fields.name: MTU
fields.desc: Maximum transmission unit field of the mapping TLV.

fields.name: Ingress IF_Num
fields.desc: Ingress interface on the target node; zero means not part of the identifier.

fields.name: Egress IF_Num
fields.desc: Egress interface on the target node; zero means not part of the identifier.
